newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's current account surplus falls.
newsitem.headline: Japan's current account surplus falls.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus plunged in July from a year ago as imports increased, but the pace of the fall is likely to slow in the future, economists said Monday.

"I'd say there is a general consensus that the current account surplus is still on a declining trend but the tempo of the shrinkage is becoming dull," said Kyohei Morita, an economist at Nomura Research Institute.

Japan's Ministry of Finance said the surplus in the current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, shrank 27.3 percent to 568.2 billion yen ($5.21 billion) in July from a year ago.
The surplus in merchandise trade alone fell 26.4 percent to 730.1 billion yen ($6.69 billion), from the same month a year earlier, the 20th successive month it has declined on a year-on-year basis.

A ministry official said the volume of imports had continued to grow at a much faster pace than that of exports, while a deficit in the services account had been expanding from Japanese travelling overseas for the summer holidays.

However, the data also showed that the month's trade surplus was the smallest for any July since the ministry began tracking comparable data in January 1985, mainly on the rebound in car exports, which grew 35.5 percent from the previous year.

"This is a special factor pushing up the overall exports. Car exports to the United States rose in reaction to a sharp drop last year as auto exports were still sluggish then from the lingering effects of the Japan-U.S. car dispute," said Shuji Shirota, an economist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics Inc.

The effects of the weakening of the yen against the dollar this past year and Japanese manufacturers completing or delaying shifts of production abroad has also given wind to the growth in exports, economists said.

The ministry official said car exports appeared to have hit a major bottom after earlier declines resulting from the manufacturers' active shifts overseas, an on-going trend which started in the second half of the 1980s.
"With the volume of exports growing again in July, the manufacturers' trend of shifting their production overseas appears to be taking a breather now," the official said.

The weaker yen may also slow down the drive by manufacturers to move production out of Japan, although economists say plans are more likely to be affected by factors like labour costs and economic growth of the country.

The yen's weakness has also helped Japanese exports regain their competitiveness, although some, like cars, may not have felt the benefit as much since their productions bases have already been moved overseas, economists said.

Meanwhile, the same currency factor has dampened inflows of imports by pushing up prices. Economists also said that sluggish consumer demand meant the domestic market for imported goods was not getting any bigger.
But the underlying trend remains unchanged. Small and medium-sized firms are still in the process of moving their output overseas, which would help growth in imports to Japan.
More shifts in production bases overseas, coupled with slower economic growth in Asia and the United States, would cap growth in exports, they said.
"Although the pace of the drop in the current account surplus will slow down, the surplus will not fall into a deficit," an economist at a research arm of a Japanese bank said.
